questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Economics is fundamentally regarded as a science of choice because it studies how
options: central banks fix the value of a nation's currency
individuals and societies allocate scarce resources among competing unlimited wants
firms design advertising campaigns to boost sales
governments regulate the activities of private firms
questions.explanation: Economics is often called the science of choice because scarcity forces individuals and societies to choose how to allocate limited resources among unlimited wants.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The central economic problem confronting every society, regardless of its political system, is that of
options: scarcity relative to unlimited human wants
excess production of consumer goods
unemployment of skilled labour alone
an oversupply of natural resources
questions.explanation: Scarcity, the imbalance between limited resources and unlimited wants, is the root economic problem that gives rise to the need for choice in every society.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: An opportunity cost arises specifically because
options: goods are always priced above their true value
resources devoted to one use cannot simultaneously be used to satisfy another want
governments impose taxes on all transactions
consumers have unlimited income to spend
questions.explanation: Opportunity cost exists because scarce resources have alternative uses; choosing one option necessarily means forgoing the next best alternative.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: A farmer with one hectare of land decides to plant maize instead of cassava. The opportunity cost of this decision is the
options: market price of the maize harvested
cassava output that would have been obtained had the land been used for cassava
cost of fertiliser used on the maize farm
labour wages paid to farm workers
questions.explanation: Opportunity cost is measured in terms of the next best alternative forgone; here, it is the cassava output sacrificed by choosing to plant maize.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The production possibility curve (PPC) of an economy illustrates
options: the amount of money in circulation in an economy
the level of taxation imposed on producers
the exact quantity of goods a country must produce
the maximum combinations of two goods that can be produced with given resources and technology
questions.explanation: The PPC shows the possible output combinations of two goods an economy can produce efficiently given fixed resources and technology, illustrating the concept of opportunity cost via its shape.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: A point lying inside (below) the production possibility curve indicates that the economy is
options: underutilising its available resources
producing an unattainable combination of goods
operating at full and efficient capacity
experiencing a shortage of raw materials only
questions.explanation: Points inside the PPC represent inefficient or underutilised resource use, since the economy could produce more of both goods by using idle or misallocated resources.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: An outward shift of the entire production possibility curve is most likely caused by
options: a rise in the general price level
an improvement in technology or an increase in available resources
an increase in the rate of unemployment
a fall in consumer income
questions.explanation: Economic growth, reflected as an outward PPC shift, results from increases in resource quantity/quality or technological advancement that raise the economy's productive capacity.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The concave (bowed-out) shape of a typical production possibility curve reflects the principle of
options: a fixed exchange rate between two goods
constant opportunity cost regardless of output combination
decreasing returns to scale in all industries
increasing opportunity cost as more of one good is produced
questions.explanation: Because resources are not perfectly adaptable between uses, producing successive units of one good requires giving up increasing amounts of the other, producing the curve's concave shape.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Which of the following best distinguishes a 'want' from a 'need' in economics?
options: A want is always more expensive than a need
A need can be satisfied while a want cannot
There is no meaningful distinction between the two in economics
A need is essential for survival while a want is a desire that adds satisfaction but is not essential
questions.explanation: Needs (e.g., food, shelter) are essential for survival, while wants are desires for goods and services that enhance wellbeing but are not strictly necessary.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Which of the following is an example of the factor of production known as 'capital'?
options: The wages paid to factory workers
A factory's machinery used to manufacture goods
The entrepreneurial skill of a business founder
The natural fertility of farmland
questions.explanation: Capital refers to man-made resources used in production, such as machinery, tools, and equipment, distinct from land, labour, and entrepreneurship.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The reward paid to the factor of production known as entrepreneurship is called
options: profit
rent
wages
interest
questions.explanation: Profit is the reward for entrepreneurship, compensating the entrepreneur for organising other factors of production and bearing business risk.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: A scale of preference becomes necessary primarily because
options: prices of goods never change
all wants can be satisfied simultaneously
government regulations require it
income and resources are limited relative to the number of wants to be satisfied
questions.explanation: Because a consumer's income cannot satisfy every want, a scale of preference ranks wants by urgency so that the most pressing ones are met first.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: In a pure market (capitalist) economy, the question of 'what to produce' is primarily answered by
options: a council of traditional rulers
an international trade organisation
a central planning authority
the interaction of consumer demand and producer supply through the price mechanism
questions.explanation: In capitalism, the price mechanism, driven by the forces of demand and supply, signals producers on what goods to produce and in what quantities.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: A key weakness often associated with a pure command (socialist) economy is
options: excessive competition among numerous private firms
the possibility of resource misallocation due to the absence of price signals
the total absence of any central authority
frequent gluts caused by uncoordinated private production
questions.explanation: Without market prices to guide production decisions, central planners may misjudge consumer preferences and resource needs, leading to shortages or surpluses.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: A traditional economic system is best described as one in which economic decisions are guided mainly by
options: multinational corporations operating freely
customs, traditions, and inherited practices passed down through generations
an elected legislature's annual budget
computerised market algorithms
questions.explanation: Traditional economies rely on long-established customs and practices, often centred on agriculture, hunting, or barter, to answer the basic economic questions.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: A major advantage claimed for a mixed economic system over a pure market economy is that it
options: eliminates the price mechanism entirely
guarantees that no firm ever earns abnormal profit
removes the need for any economic planning
allows government intervention to correct market failures while preserving private enterprise
questions.explanation: Mixed economies combine the efficiency incentives of private enterprise with government intervention to address issues like monopoly power, externalities, and inequality that pure markets fail to correct.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Under a capitalist economic system, the profit motive primarily serves to
options: ensure that government controls all major industries
guarantee equal income distribution among citizens
eliminate the need for competition
incentivise firms to produce efficiently and respond to consumer demand
questions.explanation: The pursuit of profit drives firms in a capitalist system to produce goods efficiently and in line with what consumers are willing to pay for, guiding resource allocation.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Which of the following is a distinguishing feature of a socialist economic system as opposed to capitalism?
options: Free operation of the price mechanism without government interference
Collective or state ownership of the major means of production
Reliance on private property rights as the dominant form of ownership
Unrestricted competition among numerous private firms
questions.explanation: Socialism is characterised by collective or state ownership of key productive resources, in contrast to capitalism's emphasis on private ownership.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: One criticism frequently levelled against a pure capitalist economic system is that it may lead to
options: complete elimination of consumer choice
an inability of prices to respond to demand changes
total absence of competition among firms
wide disparities in income and wealth distribution
questions.explanation: Because rewards in capitalism are tied closely to ownership of resources and market success, income and wealth can become highly unequally distributed over time.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Which measure of central tendency is most affected by extremely large or small (outlier) values in a data set?
options: The mode
The arithmetic mean
The range
The median
questions.explanation: Because the mean sums all values and divides by their count, a single extreme outlier can significantly distort it, unlike the median or mode.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Given the data set 3, 5, 5, 7, 9, 11, the mode of the data is
questions.explanation: The mode is the most frequently occurring value; 5 appears twice while every other value appears once.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The median of the data set 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12 is
questions.explanation: With six ordered values, the median is the average of the two middle values (6 and 8): (6+8)/2 = 7.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: An index number, such as the Consumer Price Index, is primarily used to
options: record the absolute quantity of goods produced in a given year
determine the exact exchange rate between two currencies
calculate a firm's total profit for the year
measure the relative change in a variable over time compared to a base period
questions.explanation: Index numbers express the value of a variable in a given period as a percentage of its value in a chosen base period, making relative changes easy to track.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: A scatter diagram in economic analysis is primarily used to
options: represent the parts of a whole as percentages
track a single variable's change over successive time periods
show the relationship or correlation between two variables
list data values in order of frequency
questions.explanation: Scatter diagrams plot paired data points for two variables, helping analysts visually detect whether a relationship (positive, negative, or none) exists between them.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: If the correlation coefficient between two variables is calculated as -0.9, this indicates
options: no relationship at all between the variables
a strong negative (inverse) relationship between the variables
that one variable causes the other with certainty
a strong positive relationship between the variables
questions.explanation: A coefficient close to -1 indicates a strong negative correlation, meaning the variables tend to move in opposite directions, though correlation alone does not prove causation.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: A histogram differs from a bar chart mainly in that a histogram
options: cannot be used to represent frequency distributions
can only display data as percentages of a total
always shows discrete categorical data with gaps between bars
is used for continuous data grouped into class intervals with no gaps between bars
questions.explanation: Histograms represent continuous, grouped numerical data with adjoining bars, whereas bar charts typically represent discrete categories with gaps between bars.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: In economic analysis, 'ceteris paribus' is an assumption meaning
options: prices are fixed permanently by law
government policy has no effect on the economy
all other relevant factors are held constant while one variable is examined
all economic variables change simultaneously
questions.explanation: 'Ceteris paribus' is a Latin phrase economists use to isolate the effect of one variable on another by assuming all other influencing factors remain unchanged.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: A movement along a fixed demand curve, as opposed to a shift of the curve, is caused specifically by
options: a change in the price of the good itself
a change in the price of a related good
a change in consumer tastes and preferences
a change in consumer income
questions.explanation: A change in the good's own price causes a movement along the existing demand curve, while changes in income, tastes, or related prices shift the entire curve.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: If the price of tea rises and, as a result, the demand for coffee increases, tea and coffee are best described as
options: complementary goods
inferior goods
substitute goods
Giffen goods
questions.explanation: Substitute goods can replace one another in consumption; a price rise in one causes consumers to switch to the other, raising the other's demand.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: An inferior good is one for which demand
options: falls as consumer income rises
can never be purchased by low-income consumers
is completely unaffected by changes in income
rises as consumer income rises
questions.explanation: Inferior goods see falling demand as income rises because consumers switch to preferred, often higher-quality substitutes once they can afford them.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The price elasticity of supply for agricultural produce is generally lower (more inelastic) in the short run mainly because
options: there are no substitutes for agricultural produce
farmers are indifferent to changes in market price
government fixes all agricultural prices
production takes a growing season and cannot be rapidly increased in response to price changes
questions.explanation: Agricultural supply cannot respond instantly to price changes because crops require a fixed growing period, making short-run supply relatively price-inelastic.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: If a 10% rise in the price of a good leads to a 20% fall in quantity demanded, the demand for the good is
options: unitary elastic
inelastic
perfectly inelastic
elastic
questions.explanation: Since the percentage change in quantity demanded (20%) exceeds the percentage change in price (10%), the elasticity coefficient exceeds 1, indicating elastic demand.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: A perfectly inelastic supply curve is best represented graphically as a line that is
options: downward-sloping from left to right
horizontal, showing supply is infinitely responsive to price
vertical, showing quantity supplied does not change regardless of price
upward-sloping at a 45-degree angle
questions.explanation: Perfectly inelastic supply means quantity supplied remains fixed no matter how price changes, producing a vertical supply curve, as with a unique painting.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Government imposition of a price ceiling below the market equilibrium price is most likely to result in
options: a persistent surplus of the good in the market
an automatic rise in the equilibrium price
a persistent shortage of the good in the market
no change in the quantity traded
questions.explanation: A price ceiling set below equilibrium keeps price artificially low, causing quantity demanded to exceed quantity supplied and creating a lasting shortage.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: A minimum wage law that sets wages above the market equilibrium wage rate is an example of a
options: subsidy
progressive tax
price ceiling
price floor
questions.explanation: A price floor is a legally set minimum price above equilibrium; a minimum wage above the market-clearing wage is a classic example, often causing a labour surplus (unemployment).

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The concept of joint demand best describes the relationship between
options: two goods that serve as substitutes for each other
goods whose supply increases together
goods that are demanded together because they are used in conjunction, such as a car and fuel
a good demanded by two different income groups
questions.explanation: Joint demand refers to complementary goods consumed together, so demand for one is linked to demand for the other, such as cars and petrol.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The law of diminishing marginal utility states that as a consumer consumes successive units of a good,
options: marginal utility remains constant no matter how much is consumed
total utility continuously decreases from the first unit onward
the price of the good automatically falls
the additional satisfaction (marginal utility) derived from each extra unit eventually decreases
questions.explanation: Diminishing marginal utility describes how the extra satisfaction from consuming one more unit of a good tends to fall as more units are consumed within a given period.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: A rational consumer maximises total utility from a fixed income by allocating spending such that
options: the marginal utility per naira spent is equalised across all goods purchased
equal quantities of every available good are purchased
all income is spent on a single good with the highest total utility
the cheapest good available is always bought exclusively
questions.explanation: The equi-marginal principle states utility is maximised when the marginal utility per unit of money spent is equal across all goods, given the consumer's budget.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Consumer surplus is best defined as the
options: tax paid by consumers on a purchased good
profit earned by a firm from selling a good
difference between what a consumer is willing to pay and what they actually pay for a good
total amount of money a consumer spends on a good
questions.explanation: Consumer surplus measures the extra benefit consumers receive when the price they actually pay is lower than the maximum price they were willing to pay.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Indifference curve analysis assumes that a consumer is indifferent between two combinations of goods when
options: one combination costs strictly less than the other
the consumer's income changes between the two combinations
both combinations contain identical quantities of each good
both combinations yield the same total level of satisfaction
questions.explanation: An indifference curve plots combinations of two goods that give a consumer equal total utility, so the consumer has no preference between any points on the curve.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: A budget line in consumer theory represents
options: all combinations of two goods a consumer can afford given fixed income and prices
the government's total revenue from taxation
the maximum utility a consumer can ever achieve
the total savings of a consumer over a year
questions.explanation: The budget line shows the various combinations of two goods that exactly exhaust a consumer's given income at prevailing prices.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: A Giffen good is unusual because
options: its demand is completely unaffected by any price change
its demand rises as its price rises, contrary to the normal law of demand
it is always a luxury good purchased by high-income earners
it has no close substitutes in the market
questions.explanation: Giffen goods are a rare exception to the law of demand where a price rise leads to increased quantity demanded, typically for staple inferior goods with a strong income effect.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Total utility is maximised at the point where
options: marginal utility is negative
total utility equals average utility
marginal utility equals zero
marginal utility is at its highest positive value
questions.explanation: Total utility reaches its peak precisely when the marginal utility of consuming one more unit falls to zero; consuming beyond this point reduces total utility.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The law of diminishing returns applies specifically in the
options: determination of a country's balance of payments
long run, when all factors of production are variable
circular flow of income between households and firms
short run, when at least one factor of production is fixed
questions.explanation: Diminishing returns occur in the short run because at least one input (e.g., land or capital) is fixed while a variable input (e.g., labour) is increased, eventually reducing additional output per extra unit.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Fixed costs of production are those costs that
options: are incurred only in the long run
disappear entirely once production begins
do not change with the level of output in the short run
vary directly and proportionately with output
questions.explanation: Fixed costs, such as rent, remain constant regardless of the quantity produced in the short run, unlike variable costs which change with output.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Average total cost (ATC) is calculated as
options: marginal cost minus average fixed cost
total fixed cost divided by total variable cost
total cost divided by the quantity of output produced
total revenue divided by total cost
questions.explanation: Average total cost is found by dividing total cost (fixed plus variable costs) by the number of units produced.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Marginal cost is defined as the
options: additional cost incurred from producing one more unit of output
total cost of all units produced
average cost of producing the first unit only
difference between total revenue and total cost
questions.explanation: Marginal cost measures the extra cost a firm incurs by producing exactly one additional unit of output.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Economies of scale refer to the
options: decline in a firm's total revenue as output increases
increase in short-run marginal cost as output rises
reduction in long-run average cost as a firm increases its scale of production
rise in fixed costs as a firm expands
questions.explanation: Economies of scale occur when expanding production allows a firm to spread costs and gain efficiencies, lowering long-run average cost per unit.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Diseconomies of scale may arise in a very large firm mainly due to
options: managerial and coordination difficulties as the organisation becomes too large and complex
improved access to bulk-buying discounts
increased specialisation of labour
a fall in the price of raw materials
questions.explanation: Beyond a certain size, firms may face rising average costs due to communication breakdowns, bureaucracy, and coordination challenges, known as diseconomies of scale.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: A firm operating in the short run will shut down production if the market price falls below its
options: average fixed cost
average variable cost
marginal revenue
total revenue
questions.explanation: In the short run, a firm should shut down if price cannot cover average variable cost, since continuing production would only add to its losses beyond fixed costs already sunk.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Specialisation and division of labour primarily increase productivity because
options: each worker produces a complete product independently
fewer workers are required to meet demand for a good
workers become more skilled and efficient by focusing on a narrow, repetitive task
wages automatically rise for all workers involved
questions.explanation: By concentrating on specific tasks, workers develop expertise and speed, reducing time lost switching between different jobs, thereby raising overall output.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: A major disadvantage of extreme division of labour in a factory setting is that it can lead to
options: monotony and reduced job satisfaction among workers
a wider range of skills for every worker
lower total output due to specialisation
greater flexibility in worker roles
questions.explanation: Repetitive, narrowly defined tasks under extreme division of labour can cause boredom and dissatisfaction, potentially reducing morale despite efficiency gains.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Perfect competition is characterised by all of the following EXCEPT
options: a single firm having significant control over the market price
homogeneous (identical) products
a large number of buyers and sellers
free entry and exit of firms
questions.explanation: Under perfect competition, no single firm can influence market price because there are many small firms selling identical products; each is a 'price taker'.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: A pure monopoly exists in a market where
options: many firms sell differentiated products
there is free entry and exit for all firms
a single firm is the sole supplier of a good with no close substitutes
a few large firms dominate the industry
questions.explanation: Monopoly describes a market structure with only one seller controlling the entire supply of a good that has no close substitutes, giving the firm significant price-setting power.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Which of the following is a common barrier to entry that helps sustain a monopoly?
options: Free and unrestricted access to production technology
Exclusive control over a key raw material or patent rights
Perfectly elastic demand for the product
A large number of competing sellers
questions.explanation: Monopolists often maintain their position through barriers such as control of essential resources, patents, licences, or high startup costs that deter new entrants.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Monopolistic competition is best described as a market structure with
options: many firms selling perfectly identical products with no branding
only one firm supplying a completely unique product
a few large firms selling identical products
many firms selling similar but differentiated products, each having some control over price
questions.explanation: Monopolistic competition features many sellers offering products that are similar but distinguished by branding, quality, or features, giving each firm limited pricing power.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Oligopoly is a market structure characterised primarily by
options: a single seller with total market control
a very large number of small firms with identical products
a few large firms dominating the market, each aware of the pricing decisions of rivals
perfect knowledge and completely free entry for all firms
questions.explanation: Oligopolies involve a small number of large, interdependent firms whose pricing and output decisions are strongly influenced by anticipated reactions from rivals.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Price discrimination by a monopolist involves
options: charging different prices to different groups of consumers for the same product, unrelated to cost differences
always charging the same uniform price to every consumer
reducing output to zero to maximise profit
selling below the cost of production to all customers
questions.explanation: Price discrimination allows a firm with market power to charge different prices to different consumer segments based on their willingness to pay, boosting profit beyond uniform pricing.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: A key condition necessary for successful price discrimination is that
options: the good must have many close substitutes
all consumers must have identical elasticities of demand
the market must be perfectly competitive
the seller must be able to prevent resale of the good between the different consumer groups
questions.explanation: If consumers charged a lower price could resell to those charged a higher price, price discrimination would collapse; preventing resale is therefore essential.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: In the long run, firms in a perfectly competitive market tend to earn
options: consistent losses that force the entire industry to shut down
profits fixed by government regulation
only normal profit, as abnormal profits attract new entrants that compete profits away
permanently high abnormal profits
questions.explanation: Because entry and exit are free in perfect competition, any abnormal (supernormal) profit attracts new firms until price falls to the level of average cost, leaving only normal profit.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Gross Domestic Product (GDP) is defined as the
options: total market value of all final goods and services produced within a country's borders in a given period
total government expenditure for a fiscal year
total income earned by a country's citizens both at home and abroad
total value of exports minus imports for a country
questions.explanation: GDP measures the value of final goods and services produced domestically within a specific time period, typically a year, regardless of who owns the producing resources.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Gross National Product (GNP) differs from GDP in that GNP includes
options: income earned by a country's citizens and firms abroad, but excludes income earned domestically by foreigners
only agricultural output of a nation
government spending exclusively
only the value of goods produced domestically
questions.explanation: GNP measures output produced by a nation's citizens and firms wherever located, adding net income from abroad to GDP and excluding income earned domestically by foreign-owned resources.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The income approach to measuring national income sums up
options: total consumer spending on final goods only
total government tax revenue collected
wages, rent, interest, and profit earned by factors of production
the value of exports alone
questions.explanation: The income method calculates national income by adding all the income payments (wages, rent, interest, profit) earned by the factors of production in generating output.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Double counting in national income accounting is avoided by using the
options: gross value of raw materials used in production
expenditure approach exclusively, ignoring all other methods
total sum of all sales transactions in the economy
value-added approach, which counts only the value added at each stage of production
questions.explanation: The value-added method sums only the incremental value contributed at each production stage, preventing intermediate goods from being counted multiple times.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Real GDP differs from nominal GDP in that real GDP is
options: measured only in foreign currency
always higher than nominal GDP
calculated without including any government spending
adjusted for changes in the price level (inflation), reflecting actual output changes
questions.explanation: Real GDP uses constant base-year prices to strip out the effect of inflation, allowing a more accurate comparison of actual output changes over time.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Per capita income is calculated by dividing
options: a country's total national income by its total population
total government revenue by total exports
total exports by total imports
total consumption by total investment
questions.explanation: Per capita income is a rough measure of average income per person, obtained by dividing total national income by the total population of the country.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Which of the following is a major limitation of using GDP alone as a measure of a nation's standard of living?
options: It cannot be calculated for developing countries
It only measures the value of imported goods
It always overstates a country's population growth rate
It does not account for income distribution or non-market activities such as unpaid household work
questions.explanation: GDP is a measure of total output, but it ignores how income is distributed among citizens and excludes valuable non-market activities like subsistence and household labour.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The circular flow of income model illustrates how
options: a central bank controls the money supply
the government sets the exchange rate for a currency
international trade balances are calculated
income flows between households and firms in exchange for factors of production and goods/services
questions.explanation: The circular flow model shows households supplying factors of production to firms in return for income, which households then spend on goods and services produced by firms, creating a continuous flow.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Money is best defined in economics as anything that is generally acceptable as a
options: measure of a country's population
store of physical labour only
substitute for all forms of collateral
medium of exchange for goods and services
questions.explanation: Money's primary function is serving as a widely accepted medium of exchange, facilitating transactions without the inefficiencies of barter.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Which of the following is NOT typically regarded as one of the main functions of money?
options: Determining a firm's total factor productivity
Acting as a store of value
Functioning as a unit of account
Serving as a medium of exchange
questions.explanation: The recognised functions of money are medium of exchange, store of value, unit of account, and standard for deferred payment — not determining productivity, which is a separate production concept.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The primary function of a central bank, such as the Central Bank of Nigeria, includes
options: regulating the money supply and acting as lender of last resort to commercial banks
setting retail prices for all goods in the economy
directly manufacturing consumer goods for export
collecting personal income tax from individual citizens
questions.explanation: Central banks control monetary policy, regulate the banking system, and act as lender of last resort, but do not engage in producing consumer goods or collecting income tax directly.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Demand-pull inflation occurs mainly when
options: aggregate demand in the economy exceeds available aggregate supply at existing prices
the cost of production inputs rises sharply
the exchange rate of the local currency appreciates
the government reduces the money supply significantly
questions.explanation: Demand-pull inflation arises when total spending in the economy grows faster than the economy's productive capacity, pulling prices upward as too much money chases too few goods.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Cost-push inflation is primarily triggered by
options: a decrease in the general price level
a rise in the cost of production, such as wages or raw materials, which firms pass on as higher prices
an increase in the supply of goods relative to demand
a fall in consumer confidence
questions.explanation: Cost-push inflation happens when rising production costs (wages, raw materials, energy) squeeze firms' margins, prompting them to raise prices to maintain profitability.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: One major consequence of persistent high inflation on an economy is that it
options: erodes the purchasing power of money and real incomes
guarantees full employment in the long run
automatically increases the real value of savings
always leads to lower interest rates
questions.explanation: As prices rise persistently, each unit of currency buys fewer goods and services, reducing the real value of money holdings, savings, and fixed incomes.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The commercial banks' ability to create credit is fundamentally based on the principle that
options: banks are legally required to lend to only one customer at a time
all deposits must be held in full as cash reserves at all times
credit creation is entirely prohibited by banking regulations
banks only need to keep a fraction of deposits as reserves and can lend out the rest
questions.explanation: Under the fractional reserve banking system, banks retain only a portion of deposits as reserves and lend out the remainder, which expands the overall money supply through repeated deposit-lending cycles.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: A rise in the Monetary Policy Rate (MPR) set by a central bank is typically intended to
options: reduce the money supply and curb inflationary pressures by making borrowing more expensive
eliminate all forms of taxation in the economy
increase the amount of currency in circulation immediately
stimulate rapid economic expansion by encouraging more borrowing
questions.explanation: Raising the policy rate increases the cost of borrowing, discouraging spending and investment, which helps to reduce inflationary pressure by contracting the money supply.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Which of the following best describes the function of the Nigeria Deposit Insurance Corporation (NDIC)?
options: It insures bank deposits to protect depositors in the event of bank failure
It sets the official exchange rate for the naira
It issues currency notes and coins for circulation
It regulates the stock exchange market
questions.explanation: The NDIC provides deposit insurance, safeguarding depositors' funds up to a specified limit if a licensed bank fails, thereby promoting confidence in the banking system.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: A progressive tax system is one in which
options: everyone pays exactly the same fixed amount of tax
the proportion of income paid as tax increases as income rises
only businesses, and not individuals, are taxed
the proportion of income paid as tax decreases as income rises
questions.explanation: Progressive taxation applies higher tax rates to higher income brackets, so wealthier individuals pay a larger percentage of their income in tax than lower earners.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Value Added Tax (VAT) is generally classified as a
options: direct tax levied solely on corporate profits
progressive tax based strictly on income level
regressive indirect tax, since it takes a larger proportion of income from lower earners
tax paid only by government agencies
questions.explanation: VAT is an indirect tax on consumption; because lower-income earners spend a larger share of their income on taxed goods, VAT tends to be regressive in effect.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Which of the following is an example of a direct tax?
options: Value Added Tax
Excise duty
Import duty
Personal income tax
questions.explanation: Direct taxes, like personal income tax and company income tax, are levied directly on the income or wealth of individuals or firms and cannot easily be shifted to others.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: A budget deficit occurs when
options: a government has no external debt
government expenditure exceeds government revenue in a given fiscal period
government revenue exactly equals government expenditure
government revenue exceeds government expenditure
questions.explanation: A budget deficit arises when a government spends more than it collects in revenue during a fiscal year, often financed through borrowing.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Public debt incurred through borrowing from foreign lenders is generally referred to as
options: budget surplus
external debt
deferred tax liability
internal debt
questions.explanation: External debt refers to money a government owes to foreign creditors, such as other governments, foreign banks, or international institutions, as opposed to internal debt owed to domestic lenders.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Deficit financing through borrowing from the central bank can potentially lead to
options: an automatic reduction in government expenditure
a permanent decrease in the general price level
an increase in the money supply and inflationary pressure
the elimination of public debt
questions.explanation: When a government borrows directly from the central bank ('printing money'), it expands the money supply, which can fuel demand-pull inflation if not matched by higher output.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Government subsidies on a good are primarily intended to
options: eliminate the good entirely from the market
increase government tax revenue directly
lower the market price of the good and encourage its consumption or production
raise the market price of the good to reduce demand
questions.explanation: A subsidy is a payment or benefit from government to producers or consumers that lowers the effective price of a good, encouraging greater production or consumption of it.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Public expenditure on building roads, schools, and hospitals is generally classified as
options: debt servicing expenditure
recurrent expenditure, since it must be repeated annually
transfer payment, since no goods or services are exchanged
capital expenditure, since it creates long-term productive assets
questions.explanation: Capital expenditure covers spending on infrastructure and durable assets that provide long-term benefits, distinguishing it from recurrent expenditure like salaries and routine running costs.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The principle of comparative advantage suggests that a country should specialise in producing goods for which it has
options: the largest population of skilled workers
complete self-sufficiency in all goods
the lowest opportunity cost of production relative to other countries
the highest absolute output regardless of cost
questions.explanation: Comparative advantage states that mutual gains from trade arise when countries specialise in goods they can produce at the lowest opportunity cost, even if another country is more efficient at producing everything.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: A tariff imposed on imported goods is primarily intended to
options: eliminate all foreign trade completely
raise the price of imports and protect domestic industries from foreign competition
lower the price of imports to benefit domestic consumers
subsidise foreign producers directly
questions.explanation: Tariffs are taxes on imports that increase their price relative to domestically produced goods, shielding local industries from cheaper foreign competition.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: An import quota differs from a tariff in that a quota
options: encourages unlimited importation of a good
always generates tax revenue for the government
applies only to exported goods, not imports
directly restricts the physical quantity of a good that can be imported, rather than taxing it
questions.explanation: While a tariff raises the price of imports through taxation, a quota sets a direct numerical limit on the quantity of a good that may be imported within a period.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: A favourable balance of trade occurs when a country's
options: currency depreciates sharply against foreign currencies
value of imports exceeds the value of its exports
value of exports exceeds the value of its imports
exports and imports are exactly equal
questions.explanation: A favourable (surplus) balance of trade exists when the monetary value of a country's exports of goods is greater than the value of its imports over a given period.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The balance of payments differs from the balance of trade in that the balance of payments
options: measures a country's total government budget deficit
records only visible merchandise trade in goods
records all economic transactions between a country and the rest of the world, including services and capital flows
applies only to trade between neighbouring countries
questions.explanation: The balance of payments is a comprehensive record covering trade in goods and services, income flows, and capital movements, whereas the balance of trade covers only visible goods.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The World Trade Organization (WTO) primarily exists to
options: coordinate monetary policy among central banks
set global exchange rates for all currencies
provide short-term loans to countries facing balance of payments crises
promote and regulate free and fair international trade among member nations
questions.explanation: The WTO establishes rules for international trade, resolves trade disputes, and works to reduce trade barriers among its member countries.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The primary role of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) is to
options: provide financial assistance and promote monetary cooperation among member countries
set global commodity prices
regulate international trade tariffs exclusively
manufacture currency for developing nations
questions.explanation: The IMF offers financial support to countries facing balance of payments difficulties and promotes international monetary cooperation and exchange rate stability.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: ECOWAS (Economic Community of West African States) was established mainly to promote
options: restrictions on trade between member states
regional economic integration and cooperation among West African countries
a single global currency for all countries
military alliances between African and European nations
questions.explanation: ECOWAS aims to foster economic integration, free movement of goods and people, and cooperation among West African member states to boost regional development.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: A depreciation of a country's currency relative to other currencies is likely to make its exports
options: cheaper and more competitive in foreign markets
illegal to sell abroad
unaffected in price for foreign buyers
more expensive for foreign buyers
questions.explanation: Currency depreciation lowers the foreign-currency price of a country's exports, generally making them more attractive and competitive to buyers abroad.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The Nigerian economy has historically been described as heavily dependent on
options: manufactured electronics exports
agricultural exports exclusively, with no other sector contributing
crude oil exports as its major source of foreign exchange earnings
revenue from tourism alone
questions.explanation: Since the 1970s oil boom, Nigeria's economy has relied heavily on crude oil exports for the bulk of its foreign exchange earnings and a significant share of government revenue.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The 'Dutch Disease' phenomenon, often discussed in relation to Nigeria's economy, refers to
options: the decline of other productive sectors, such as agriculture and manufacturing, due to overreliance on a booming resource sector like oil
excessive foreign direct investment in the health sector
a currency crisis caused by trade with the Netherlands
a public health epidemic affecting the labour force
questions.explanation: 'Dutch Disease' describes how a booming natural resource sector (like oil) can cause currency appreciation and neglect of other sectors, weakening broader economic diversification.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The Structural Adjustment Programme (SAP) introduced in Nigeria in 1986 was primarily aimed at
options: fixing the naira permanently to the US dollar
abolishing the Central Bank of Nigeria
restructuring the economy away from oil dependence and reducing government intervention in markets
nationalising all foreign-owned businesses in Nigeria
questions.explanation: SAP, guided by IMF/World Bank recommendations, sought to liberalise the Nigerian economy, reduce reliance on oil, and cut back extensive government control over economic activities.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Which of the following best describes the informal sector's role in the Nigerian economy?
options: It consists solely of large multinational corporations
It contributes nothing to national output
It is entirely regulated and taxed like the formal sector
It employs a significant proportion of the workforce, often operating outside formal regulation and taxation
questions.explanation: Nigeria's informal sector, comprising small-scale trading, artisanal work, and unregistered businesses, absorbs a large share of the labour force despite limited regulation and tax compliance.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Nigeria's transition from a fixed to a more flexible exchange rate regime for the naira has generally been intended to
options: allow market forces to determine the naira's value and improve foreign exchange market efficiency
guarantee the naira always appreciates against the dollar
eliminate the need for a central bank
permanently peg the naira to the price of crude oil
questions.explanation: Moving toward a more market-determined exchange rate allows demand and supply for foreign currency to guide the naira's value, aiming to reduce distortions from an artificially fixed rate.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Underemployment in the Nigerian labour market refers to a situation where
options: the entire workforce is fully and optimally employed
workers are employed in jobs that do not fully utilise their skills or provide adequate working hours/income
only foreign workers are employed in the economy
workers are completely without any job or income
questions.explanation: Underemployment describes workers who are technically employed but in roles below their qualification level, working fewer hours than desired, or earning insufficient income.
